transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
At a G20 foreign ministers meeting in Atlanta, Secretary of State Marco Rubio says he had a chance to meet briefly with Brazil's foreign minister.
And here's Michelle Kellerman reports, President Trump still hasn't recognized the recent election results there.
Secretary Rubio says he had a couple of brief interactions with his Brazilian counterpart,
and he made it sound like normal diplomatic encounters, as did the Brazilians.
But these are tense times less than a week after right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro lost a run-off and fled to the U.S., claiming fraud.
Rubio says the U.S. government was not involved in the travel arrangements.
The president made clear that if he arrived in the United States in a port of entry, that he would be paroled into the country, and he was.
Brazil is a member of the Group of 20.
This foreign ministers meeting was meant to plan for a summit next month in Florida,
and President Luis Ignacio Lula da Silva is expected to attend.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, Atlanta.
The Justice Department's lawsuit in the Alaska U.S. Senate election over possible voter confusion,
because two candidates have similar names, continues with a new wrinkle.
And here's Ryan Lucas says more.
The department wants the court to delay certification in the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses by a small margin.
That's because there's another Dan Sullivan on the ballot, and the argument is that having two people with the same name could confuse voters.
The state Supreme Court already ruled that both Sullivans could run.
Things seemed to have settled down until a New York Times report this week that said Democrats recruited the second Dan Sullivan to run,
specifically to siphon votes away from the Republican.
The Justice Department revised its lawsuit to include those allegations.
Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation.
The Justice Department already has a criminal investigation underway.
And here's Ryan Lucas.
Democratic candidate Mary Peltola denies the New York Times allegations.
And with election day just days away, political campaigns are making their final push for votes.
And increasingly, that means sending text messages directly to your cell phone.
Texas Public Radio's David Martin Davies says more.
Travis Trawick is the founder and CEO of Full Pack, which specializes in political text messaging.
He says these texts target voters based on their demographics, political interest, and voting history.
I know precisely who I'm going to engage with.
I can send a message straight to their phone directly to their pocket.
Artificial intelligence is also allowing campaigns to refine their pitches.
You can curate that in so many different ways and really slice those audiences to be as small as possible.
And as Tuesday approaches, texting campaigns are becoming more aggressive.
If it becomes too much for you, voters can reply with the word stop to opt out of a list.
For NPR News, I'm David Martin Davies.
You're listening to NPR News.
A pair of new blood tests can help doctors determine whether a patient may have Alzheimer's disease.
John Hamilton reports the tests offer an alternative to expensive brain scans.
The blood tests measure a protein called PTOW 217.
It's closely associated with the presence of amyloid plaques in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer's.
Dr. David Holtzman of Washington University School of Medicine helped develop the approach.
That particular test is extremely accurate at determining whether you have amyloid in the brain or not.
Nearly as good as a costly PET scan.
Holtzman says the new blood tests are meant for older people who are already experiencing problems with memory and thinking,
not people who are just curious about their brain health.
They were approved by the Food and Drug Administration this summer.
For NPR News, I'm John Hamilton.
Some 200 cruise ship passengers on an around-the-world voyage that promoted its cabins as floating homes
are now scrambling for other accommodations after the MV Odyssey said it can't afford the gas to sail the ship.
The ship set sail two years ago on a voyage to seven continents, offering in ads to make the Odyssey a permanent home.
But without warning this week, passengers, mostly Americans, were given hours to clean out their cabins and disembark in Cambodia.
The fate of the ship is uncertain, and some passengers say they sold their homes to buy a ticket on the ship, which starts at around $230,000.
Daylight saving time ends overnight at 2 a.m. for most of the country, and that's when we set the clocks back one hour.
I'm Janine Hurst, NPR News.
This message comes from Designer Shoe Warehouse.
You know that feeling when you find shoes you love at a great price and want to tell everyone about it?
Find something to brag about at Designer Shoe Warehouse, like the latest styles from brands you love,
the trends everyone's obsessing over, and shoes that make you feel like you.
Head to a DSW store or dsw.com today for shoes that get you at prices that get your budget.
DSW. Let us surprise you.

topics.text: Secretary Rubio briefly meets Brazil's foreign minister at G20 meeting in Atlanta amid tensions over Bolsonaro
Justice Department lawsuit in Alaska Senate race seeks delayed certification over second Dan Sullivan on ballot
Campaigns send aggressive targeted text messages to voters ahead of Tuesday's election, Texas Public Radio reports
New FDA-approved blood tests help doctors detect amyloid plaques linked to Alzheimer's, offering alternative to PET scans
Around-the-world cruise MV Odyssey strands about 200 passengers in Cambodia after ship can't afford fuel
Daylight saving time ends overnight, with clocks set back one hour for most of the country
